reason: Both sources thoroughly document TON 618's discovery, extreme luminosity, nebula size, and competing mass estimates.
story: In 1957, astronomers scanning photographic plates in Mexico catalogued a faint, violet point of light and labeled it entry 618 in the Tonantzintla Catalogue, assuming it was an ordinary faint blue star. Thirteen years later, radio dishes in Bologna and spectrographs at McDonald Observatory revealed something terrifying. TON 618 was not a faint galactic neighbor, but an active quasar 10.8 billion light-years in lookback distance, shining as brilliantly as 140 trillion Suns and completely drowning out its host galaxy. At its heart lies an ultramassive black hole spanning 1,300 astronomical units across its event horizon—more than 40 times Pluto's distance from the Sun. Spectroscopic measurements of infalling gas whipping around at over 10,000 kilometers per second yielded an astonishing mass estimate of 66 billion solar masses, recently revised to 40.7 billion. Wrapped in a glowing hydrogen nebula over 300,000 light-years across, this ancient monster remains one of the heaviest singular objects in the universe.
angle: A faint violet speck catalogued in 1957 as an ordinary blue star turned out to be an ultramassive black hole up to 66 billion times the mass of our Sun, with an event horizon 40 times wider than Pluto's orbit.

claims.claim: TON 618 was first discovered in 1957 during a survey of faint blue stars by Mexican astronomers Braulio Iriarte and Enrique Chavira.
The object was initially recorded using a Schmidt telescope at the Tonantzintla Observatory in Mexico.
It was catalogued as entry number 618 in the Tonantzintla Catalogue.
TON 618 appeared distinctly violet or faint blue on photographic survey plates.
Because quasars were not recognized until 1963, TON 618's true nature was initially unknown.
In 1970, a radio survey in Bologna, Italy detected radio emissions from TON 618.
Marie-Helene Ulrich obtained optical spectra of TON 618 at the McDonald Observatory, confirming it as a distant quasar.
Spectroscopic measurements established TON 618's emission redshift at z = 2.219.
The light from TON 618 has taken approximately 10.8 billion years to travel to Earth.
The comoving distance from Earth to TON 618 is approximately 18.2 billion light-years.
TON 618 has an absolute magnitude of approximately -30.7.
The quasar shines with an extreme luminosity equivalent to 140 trillion Suns.
The host galaxy of TON 618 cannot be directly imaged from Earth because the central quasar completely outshines it.
Gas in TON 618's broad-line region travels at orbital speeds exceeding 10,000 kilometers per second.
Virial mass measurements using the H-beta spectral line yielded a black hole mass estimate of 66 billion solar masses.
At 66 billion solar masses, the black hole's Schwarzschild radius spans approximately 1,300 astronomical units.
Subsequent mass estimates analyzing the C IV emission line revised the black hole's mass down to approximately 40.7 billion solar masses.
TON 618 is surrounded by an enormous Lyman-alpha gas nebula spanning at least 100 kiloparsecs across.
ALMA millimeter-array observations detected a massive molecular outflow and circumgalactic cold gas reservoir surrounding TON 618.
TON 618 is classified as a radio-loud quasar.

disputed: Black hole mass: older widely cited estimates derived from H-beta lines place the mass at 66 billion solar masses, whereas newer C IV measurements estimate 40.7 billion solar masses (script should explicitly state both figures or attribute the revision).

Telescope aperture: S1 states the 1957 discovery used a 0.7-meter Schmidt telescope, while S2 states a 50-centimeter Schmidt telescope (script should refer generally to the Schmidt telescope at Tonantzintla Observatory without naming the exact aperture size).
